From the ninth-century Irish poem Pangur Bán and I at work, Adepts, equals, cat and clerk: His whole instinct is to hunt, Mine to free the meaning pent. More than loud acclaim, I love Books, silence, thought, my alcove. Happy for me, Pangur Bán Child-plays round some mouse’s den. Truth to tell, just being here, Housed alone, housed together, Adds up to its own reward: Concentration, stealthy art. Next thing an unwary mouse Bares his flank: Pangur pounces. Next thing lines that held and held Meaning back begin to yield. All the while, his round bright eye Fixes on the wall, while I Focus my less piercing gaze On the challenge of the page. With his unsheathed, perfect nails Pangur springs, exults and kills. When the longed-for, difficult Answers come, I too exult. So it goes. To each his own. No vying. No vexation. Taking pleasure, taking pains, Kindred spirits, veterans. Day and night, soft purr, soft pad, Pangur Bán has learned his trade. Day and night, my own hard work Solves the cruxes, makes a mark.

outputs.L1:
**From the ninth-century Irish poem “Pangur Bán”**

Pangur Bán and I at work,  
Adepts and equals, cat and clerk:  
His whole instinct is to hunt;  
Mine, to free the meaning pent.

More than loud acclaim, I love  
Books, silence, thought, my alcove.  
Happy for me, Pangur Bán  
Child-plays round some mouse’s den.

Truth to tell, our being here—  
Housed alone, yet housed together—  
Adds up to its own reward:  
Concentration, stealthy art.

Then an unwary mouse, at last,  
Bares his flank: Pangur pounces.  
Then the lines that held and held  
Meaning back begin to yield.

All the while, his bright, round eye  
Fixes on the wall, while I  
Focus my less piercing gaze  
On the challenge of the page.

With his perfect, unsheathed nails,  
Pangur springs, exults, and kills.  
When the longed-for, difficult  
Answers come, I too exult.

So it goes: to each his own.  
No vying and no vexation.  
Taking pleasure, taking pains—  
Kindred spirits, veterans.

Day and night, with purr and pad,  
Pangur Bán has learned his trade.  
Day and night, my own hard work  
Solves the cruxes, makes its mark.
outputs.L2:
Inspired by the ninth-century Irish poem:

Pangur Bán and I pursue  
our separate crafts as practiced peers—  
he, the cat, driven to catch prey;  
I, the scholar, striving to release  
the sense imprisoned in a text.

I prefer quiet rooms, reflection,  
and books to any public praise.  
Meanwhile, Pangur happily toys  
beside the hiding place of a mouse.

Honestly, our shared solitude—  
alone, yet keeping company—  
is reward enough:  
both our arts demand patience,  
attention, and secrecy.

Suddenly a careless mouse  
exposes its side, and Pangur leaps.  
Just as suddenly, stubborn lines  
begin to surrender the meaning  
they had long concealed.

His bright, circular eye  
remains trained upon the wall;  
my weaker vision stays fixed  
on the puzzle set by the page.

With flawless claws extended,  
Pangur bounds forward, kills,  
and celebrates his success.  
When the elusive solution  
finally comes to me,  
I rejoice as well.

This is our life: each follows  
his own calling without rivalry  
or resentment. Both of us  
find delight in demanding labor,  
seasoned workers of a similar spirit.

Through every day and night,  
with quiet paws and gentle purring,  
Pangur Bán perfects his profession.  
And through every day and night,  
my persistent effort untangles  
difficult passages and leaves its trace.
outputs.L3:
The speaker compares his scholarly work with Pangur Bán’s instinctive pursuit of mice, presenting himself and the cat as equally skilled practitioners of different crafts. While Pangur devotes himself to hunting, the speaker patiently studies difficult texts. Both find fulfillment in solitude, quiet concentration, and the careful practice of their abilities.

The poem draws a clear parallel between their moments of success. Pangur’s sudden capture of a mouse resembles the scholar’s intellectual breakthrough when a difficult line finally becomes clear. These achievements are not accidental but result from sustained attention and disciplined effort. Neither the cat nor the clerk is distracted by rivalry or discouraged by frustration; instead, each takes pleasure in the work itself and quietly celebrates success.

Through constant practice, Pangur sharpens his hunting instincts, while the speaker improves his ability to interpret texts and solve scholarly problems. In this way, both leave evidence of their mastery: Pangur through his successful catches and the scholar through the understanding and intellectual mark he brings to the texts he studies.
outputs.L4:
The poem “Pangur Bán” presents a quiet parallel between a scholar and his white cat, Pangur. While the scholar spends the night studying difficult texts and searching for their hidden meaning, the cat patiently watches for mice. Their tasks are very different, yet both require solitude, concentration, and skill. The scholar carefully follows words and ideas until a difficult passage becomes clear, just as Pangur silently tracks his prey and waits for the right moment to strike.

Neither the scholar nor the cat is distracted by the outside world. Each is content to work alone and has become highly practiced in his chosen craft. Pangur takes pleasure in catching a mouse, while the scholar experiences a similar satisfaction when he solves an intellectual problem or understands a challenging text. Their success comes not from haste but from patience, discipline, and sustained attention.

By comparing scholarly study with a cat’s hunt, the poem gives equal dignity to both activities. The scholar recognizes in Pangur a companion whose habits resemble his own, despite the obvious differences between them. Both are absorbed in purposeful work, and both find fulfillment in mastering it. The poem therefore suggests that focused labor can be rewarding in itself and that a sense of kinship can arise between individuals who share the same dedication, even when their pursuits are entirely different.
outputs.L5:
### Pangur Bán

From an ancient Irish poem comes Pangur Bán, a white cat who lived beside a quiet scholar. While the scholar searched for meaning in difficult words, Pangur hunted mice in the shadows. Each worked patiently, absorbed in a different task. The scholar rejoiced when he captured an idea, just as Pangur delighted in catching his prey. Together, they became an enduring image of companionship, concentration, and the simple pleasure of doing one’s work well.

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you quote the poem about a monk working at his manuscripts while his white cat, Pangur Bán, hunts mice?
counterfactuals.output:
The poem is **“Pangur Bán,”** written by an anonymous ninth-century Irish monk. Here is Whitley Stokes’s public-domain prose translation:

> I and white Pangur practise each of us his special art: his mind is set on hunting, my mind on my special craft.  
>
> I love—it is better than all fame—to be quiet beside my book, diligently pursuing knowledge. White Pangur does not envy me: he loves his childish craft.  
>
> When the two of us—this tale never wearies us—are alone together in our house, we have something to which we may apply our skill, an endless sport.  
>
> It is usual, at times, by feats of valour, that a mouse sticks in his net, while into my net there falls some difficult problem of hard meaning.  
>
> He points his full shining eye against the enclosing wall; I point my full feeble eye against the keenness of science.  
>
> He rejoices with swift movement when a mouse sticks in his sharp claw; I too rejoice when I have grasped a problem difficult and dearly loved.  
>
> Though we are thus at all times, neither hinders the other: each of us likes his own craft, rejoicing by himself therein.  
>
> He is a master of the work which he does every day; while I am at my own work to bring difficulty to clearness.

counterfactuals.output:
The poem is **“Pangur Bán,”** an anonymous ninth-century Old Irish poem written by a monk about his white cat. Here is Kuno Meyer’s public-domain translation:

### Pangur Bán

I and Pangur Bán, my cat,  
’Tis a like task we are at;  
Hunting mice is his delight,  
Hunting words I sit all night.

Better far than praise of men  
’Tis to sit with book and pen;  
Pangur bears me no ill-will,  
He too plies his simple skill.

’Tis a merry thing to see  
At our tasks how glad are we,  
When at home we sit and find  
Entertainment to our mind.

Oftentimes a mouse will stray  
In the hero Pangur’s way;  
Oftentimes my keen thought set  
Takes a meaning in its net.

’Gainst the wall he sets his eye  
Full and fierce and sharp and sly;  
’Gainst the wall of knowledge I  
All my little wisdom try.

When a mouse darts from its den,  
O how glad is Pangur then!  
O what gladness do I prove  
When I solve the doubts I love!

So in peace our task we ply,  
Pangur Bán, my cat, and I;  
In our arts we find our bliss,  
I have mine and he has his.

Practice every day has made  
Pangur perfect in his trade;  
I get wisdom day and night,  
Turning darkness into light.
